title: Caring volunteers
hookLine: visiting the sick, preparing the dead, feeding mourners
tomorrow: Noa's first paycheck. why would anyone hand back a tenth?

cards: Hospital rooms have their own sound: the beep, the curtain on its track, the TV nobody is watching. Visiting means standing in that doorway with no idea what to say. The Talmud has a story for the doorway.
One of Rabbi Akiva's students fell sick, and none of the sages came to see him. Akiva went himself. What did he do there?
He must have talked. But the Talmud names what made the difference: they swept the floor and sprinkled it with water. The student got well and told him: Rabbi, you brought me back to life.

teach.b: From there, Akiva taught: whoever doesn't visit the sick is like someone who sheds blood. Strong words. Now the argument, and it's a real one.
One side says the visit itself heals. The Talmud, on the same page, says a visitor takes away a sixtieth of the sickness. Company is medicine: sit, listen, stay.

teach.h: THE OTHER: SEE WHAT THEY NEED.
teach.b: The other side points at the broom. Later teachers, the code called the Shulchan Aruch among them, say the heart of the mitzvah is seeing what the sick person needs, and asking mercy for them.
A pleasant chat with dust still on the floor misses it. The best case for each? For presence: a lonely person may need a face more than a favor, and nobody else came to Akiva's student at all.
For help: comfort that costs nothing can end up being about the visitor, and Akiva didn't only show up; he cleaned. A visit can hold both, one hand on the broom and one ear open.
And Jewish communities have caring volunteers who reach past the hospital.

teach.h: THE HOLY SOCIETY, THE FIRST MEAL.
teach.b: The chevra kadisha, the holy society, prepares the dead for burial with quiet care.
Neighbors bring mourners their first meal after the funeral, so nobody grieving has to cook.

how: Many Jewish communities have bikur cholim groups that visit the sick, a chevra kadisha that prepares the dead for burial, and neighbors who bring the mourners' first meal after the funeral.

games.q: your friend says a visit is about being there; chores are for nurses. what's the best case for the other side?
o: the heart of the visit is seeing what the person needs, the way Akiva's floor got swept.
the Talmud says long conversations tire the sick, so visits should be silent.
visitors can spread illness, so helping from a distance is the only safe kind.
games.why: the Shulchan Aruch says the heart of the mitzvah is seeing to the sick person's needs and asking mercy for them. the visit and the broom belong together.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one line to someone who is sick or grieving. Not advice: just that you're thinking of them, or one practical offer, a meal, a ride, a sweep of the kitchen.
Read it slowly once, and let your breath settle while you decide whether it goes in a card or a text.

wordCard.voice: Caring volunteers: the people who visit the sick, prepare the dead and feed the mourners. In Akiva's story, the broom and the visit come together.

orig.note: Hebrew: visiting the sick, a mitzvah the whole community shares.

carryVoice: Your line: hands of the community, at the bedside and at the mourners' door. Day three, done.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud Nedarim 39b–40a (a visitor takes away a sixtieth of the illness; Akiva visits his student, the floor is swept and sprinkled; 'whoever does not visit the sick is like one who sheds blood')
Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 335:4 (the main point of visiting is to see to the sick person's needs and to pray for them)
Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 378 (the meal of condolence for mourners)
